summary:
Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide under the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, which passed the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and was signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916. The 2014 statute invalidates any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex and carries a maximum federal penalty of up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Akwa Ibom stands under that secular national framework. The state lies outside the twelve states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, so the death-penalty layer does not reach it and the ceiling for same-sex sexual activity in Akwa Ibom is 14 years' imprisonment.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression and sex characteristics (June 2025) records that the national criminal framework applies across all states, and documents countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. The same note confirms that the Shari'a penal codes of the twelve states remain in force, with penalties for same-sex conduct ranging from lashes or caning up to death by stoning.

Entry screening is a live risk. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, and notes that the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act reaches participants and guests at same-sex weddings, not only the couple.

Gender identity carries no legal recognition in Nigerian law, and the statute books contain no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. A visitor therefore has no protective instrument to invoke in Akwa Ibom, whether in a police encounter, an accommodation dispute or a medical setting.

No state-specific enforcement divergence from the national position is documented for Akwa Ibom in the sources on file.
tangentialFactors:
The contrast with the Shari'a states is stark and worth holding in view when reading Akwa Ibom's 14-year ceiling. The UK Home Office note records that a Shari'a court in Bauchi sentenced three men to death by stoning in 2022, a sentence that could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and reports a further death-by-stoning sentence from Bauchi in May 2024. In January 2014 a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial.

The ceiling in the southern states is statutory rather than doctrinal, but it sits on the same enforcement machinery. The Home Office records arrests, detention and mob violence as countrywide patterns, which is to say they are not confined to the religious-criminal-code states.

Nigeria's position is reinforced by external travel advisories rather than softened by them. The FCDO warning of attacks, blackmail and intimidation aligns with the domestic picture, so a trans visitor should not read the absence of a death penalty in Akwa Ibom as evidence of a tolerant environment.
localsOnly:
Residents of Akwa Ibom live under the same 2014 statute as visitors, with the added exposure of having nowhere to relocate to legally within the country outside the twelve Shari'a states, and no state-level protection machinery in Akwa Ibom itself.

Because the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act criminalises cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations under national law, ordinary domestic arrangements and community organising carry criminal exposure for residents as well as guests.

Human Rights Watch has documented police use of the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest, which means the statute functions as an open mandate for extortion and force against residents suspected of same-sex conduct, independent of any conviction.

The absence of legal gender recognition affects residents most acutely, since documents, institutional placement and everyday interaction with state services are governed by sex markers the legal system does not permit a person to change.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, reported by Reuters in September 2022, have been enacted into law is unresolved in the sources available here. Nigeria's position on gender expression may therefore be stricter than the statutory text on file suggests.

No enforcement data specific to Akwa Ibom is sourced. The state's position is derived from its placement outside the Shari'a-code states, and the claim that no state-specific divergence exists rests on the absence of reporting rather than on a positive finding.

The conditions of placement for trans detainees in Nigerian prisons remain unsettled beyond the single documented case of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), whose assignment between male and female sections was left to official discretion, and whose detention in a maximum-security facility was found in an October 2024 panel review to violate the Nigerian Correctional Service Act. Whether that finding changed practice is not sourced.

Reporting on the August 2024 killing of the transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama records no suspects charged six months later; the current status of that investigation is not sourced here.
